title: Obsidian is the missing piece that makes Gemini and Gemini Notebook actually usable
excerpt: I added Obsidian to Gemini Notebook and Gemini, and my digital brain clicked
content_html:
Published Sep 5, 2026, 8:30 AM EDT

I cover Android with a focus on productivity, automation, and Google’s ecosystem, including Gemini and everyday apps. With a background in engineering and software development, I tend to go beyond surface-level tips and focus on how features fit into real workflows.
Before joining AP, I wrote for tech publications such as Gizbot in 2023 and iJunkie (formerly known as iPhoneHacks) from 2021 to 2022.

Gemini Notebook (formerly called NotebookLM) and Gemini already make a powerful pair.

One is a summarizing tool that knows the context of your documents, and the other is an assistant that handles everything outside that bubble.

However, when I added Obsidian to the mix, something clicked.

My system originated from the challenge of managing my drafts, notes, references, and thoughts effectively.

Gemini Notebook could explain what I uploaded, and Gemini could help me think through it, but I still had nowhere to store my ideas. Obsidian became the missing layer.

Here's how the combination of Gemini Notebook, Gemini, and Obsidian has become the most productive system I've ever built.

Gemini Notebook is my research engine

It only works with the sources I give it

Gemini Notebook's biggest strength is that it only uses the sources you upload.

If I add a book chapter, a set of PDFs, or my own notes, it works with the material I give it. That makes it useful for deep reading and long-form work.

I load it up with PDFs, saved web pages, transcripts, or Google Docs.

After everything's in, Gemini Notebook builds a workspace where every answer cites where it found the information, which means I can trust it to stay factual instead of hallucinating.

If I'm reading a long scientific paper, I can ask questions, and Gemini Notebook pulls quotes from the document, gives me a clear explanation, and highlights the section it came from.

However, Gemini Notebook has limits. It is not intended for long-term storage, linking, or cross-referencing. After a few days of working inside a notebook, it becomes a sealed chamber of ideas.

And that's where Gemini comes in.

Gemini fills the gaps between sources

It helps me understand what I'm missing

Gemini Notebook works best when I've gathered the material. Gemini helps when I don't know what I need.

When I'm writing about a topic, Gemini helps me explore angles that aren't in my uploaded sources. And when I want quick checks, comparisons, or brainstorming, Gemini is the assistant I talk to.

For instance, while working on a piece about attention management, I had summaries in Gemini Notebook and some notes on habit loops and cognitive load.

But I kept seeing references to a newer study on task switching that I hadn't saved. I asked Gemini to explain the methodology in plain English and compare it to earlier research. Then, I imported it into Gemini Notebook for deeper work.

But even with all that power, Gemini doesn't solve everything. It can analyze and explain, but it doesn't give me a long-term structure for my knowledge base.

And that's why Obsidian became the third essential piece.

Obsidian helps connect the dots

It's the missing link that puts it all together

The moment I started saving the output into Obsidian, everything changed.

Instead of losing ideas to chat histories, I now had a place for everything. It included summaries from Gemini Notebook, research ideas from Gemini, notes I'd made while reading, and connections I didn't want to forget.

Obsidian became the layer that glues everything together.

Its vault structure means every note stays in the same ecosystem. Backlinks and tags help me link concepts that would usually be saved in separate chats.

When Gemini Notebook gives me a great explanation of a character arc, or Gemini helps me understand a new concept, it goes into a permanent note. I don't have to rebuild the context when I revisit a topic later, since Obsidian already holds it.

How the loop works in practice

Obsidian is my mind map

The real magic of using Gemini Notebook, Gemini, and Obsidian together only becomes obvious when I'm deep into something complex, like working through a dense nonfiction book.

I start with Gemini Notebook. I export the chapters to PDF through Calibre or pull them into Google Docs so that Gemini Notebook can read them.

Inside the notebook, I ask it to generate character lists, chapter breakdowns, summaries, timelines, and explanations. When I'm done, I move the most useful pieces into Obsidian.

When I want to explore something deeper, such as a psychological model or a historical event, I switch to Gemini. This is where it fills the gap between what I read and what I understand.

When I get something valuable out of Gemini, it goes into Obsidian.

Obsidian is where the ideas from the book and the connections I explored with Gemini turn into something usable. I drop all my notes into my vault, cross-link them to older notes on similar themes, and create concept maps.

Tips for getting more out of the Obsidian + Gemini Notebook + Gemini setup

Take your productivity to the next level

To make this three-app workflow feel seamless, a few small habits can make a massive difference.

First, standardize how you feed information into Gemini Notebook. Consistently name your book URLs, PDFs, and personal notes.

Another underrated trick is to create a dedicated Inbox note in Obsidian. Anytime Gemini Notebook generates something worth keeping, whether it is a summary, a timeline, or a concept breakdown, I paste it into the Inbox.

Later, during a weekly cleanup session, I sort those notes into permanent homes. It prevents clutter and keeps my vault tidy without slowing down my learning flow.

When I listen to audio overviews in Gemini Notebook, I pair them with Obsidian's Daily Notes feature. Then, I jot down my thoughts or questions in the day's Obsidian notes. Later, I can turn those passing thoughts into linked notes, which builds a web of connected insights.

Finally, I leaned into Obsidian's linking system. Every time Gemini or Gemini Notebook introduces a new idea, I create a note for it and link it to related concepts in my vault.

The trio that works better together

Gemini Notebook and Gemini are strong on their own. But when Obsidian enters the mix, the dynamic changes.

Now, I have a workflow that connects everything and keeps everything accessible beyond notebooks and chats.

This combination feels unstoppable because it's sustainable. The three-app loop of Gemini Notebook, Gemini, and Obsidian keeps my work more organized for the long term.

How the loop works in practice

Obsidian is my mind map

The real magic of using Gemini Notebook, Gemini, and Obsidian together only becomes obvious when I'm deep into something complex, like working through a dense nonfiction book.

I start with Gemini Notebook. I export the chapters to PDF through Calibre or pull them into Google Docs so that Gemini Notebook can read them.

Inside the notebook, I ask it to generate character lists, chapter breakdowns, summaries, timelines, and explanations. When I'm done, I move the most useful pieces into Obsidian.

When I want to explore something deeper, such as a psychological model or a historical event, I switch to Gemini. This is where it fills the gap between what I read and what I understand.

When I get something valuable out of Gemini, it goes into Obsidian.

Obsidian is where the ideas from the book and the connections I explored with Gemini turn into something usable. I drop all my notes into my vault, cross-link them to older notes on similar themes, and create concept maps.

Tips for getting more out of the Obsidian + Gemini Notebook + Gemini setup

Take your productivity to the next level

To make this three-app workflow feel seamless, a few small habits can make a massive difference.

First, standardize how you feed information into Gemini Notebook. Consistently name your book URLs, PDFs, and personal notes.

Another underrated trick is to create a dedicated Inbox note in Obsidian. Anytime Gemini Notebook generates something worth keeping, whether it is a summary, a timeline, or a concept breakdown, I paste it into the Inbox.

Later, during a weekly cleanup session, I sort those notes into permanent homes. It prevents clutter and keeps my vault tidy without slowing down my learning flow.

When I listen to audio overviews in Gemini Notebook, I pair them with Obsidian's Daily Notes feature. Then, I jot down my thoughts or questions in the day's Obsidian notes. Later, I can turn those passing thoughts into linked notes, which builds a web of connected insights.

Finally, I leaned into Obsidian's linking system. Every time Gemini or Gemini Notebook introduces a new idea, I create a note for it and link it to related concepts in my vault.

The trio that works better together

Gemini Notebook and Gemini are strong on their own. But when Obsidian enters the mix, the dynamic changes.

Now, I have a workflow that connects everything and keeps everything accessible beyond notebooks and chats.

This combination feels unstoppable because it's sustainable. The three-app loop of Gemini Notebook, Gemini, and Obsidian keeps my work more organized for the long term.
